vignette: Thomas had spent most of his life walking the long, dim corridors of the courthouse he guarded, his footsteps echoing against the marble floors, his badge humming in the pocket of his jacket. He was seventy-one, married to Ruth for forty years, and he still found the ritual of standing on the watchtower each night comforting in its predictability. The world around him, once a familiar maze of offices and courts, was forever altered on a gray spring morning when a terrorist gunman stormed the building. A sudden burst of gunfire shattered the quiet, the crack of a nearby explosive shuddered the walls, and the air filled with the metallic scent of fear. Thomas was standing on the second floor, watching a crowd of officers flee as a bullet ricocheted off the concrete. He saw the assailant's face, a contorted grin beneath a black mask, and then the flash of the weapon. When the blast hit, the courthouse shook, and Thomas felt a hot wave of adrenaline flood his chest. He heard the shrieks of his colleagues, saw the blackened doorway, and in a split second realized the terror that would haunt him forever. After the attack, Thomas's own appraisal of the event spiraled into a harsh judgment of himself. He told himself he could not handle even the slightest upset, that his nerves had failed him in that one crucial moment. He compared himself to the younger officers who had somehow managed to keep calm, convinced that they were less prone to panic. He believed, with the conviction of a man who had lost his sense of control, that he had failed in the most important role of his life-protecting the courthouse and the people inside. These negative appraisals did not simply sit in his mind; they guided his every action. When he could not accept that he had simply reacted under unimaginable pressure, he chose a posture of defense that felt physically reassuring: he would sit with his back pressed against the wall of the security office, feeling the solid surface against his spine as a shield against the imagined threat that might still be lurking. By keeping his back to the wall, he felt he could see the entire room, every doorway, every corner, as if that would grant him a way to monitor the world more thoroughly and avoid becoming a victim again. This strategy of posture, hypervigilance, and a mind constantly rehearsing a revenge scenario became the foundation of how he tried to live after the attack. The way Thomas positioned himself in the office had a profound effect on his memory of the day. The very act of sitting rigidly with his back against the wall created a frame that made the world feel static. He could replay vivid images of the gunman's mask, the flash of the explosion, and the trembling of the walls in perfect detail, but when he tried to describe what had happened, the story refused to flow. He found himself recalling the sound of the siren that had been cut off by the gunfire, the brief flash of the bullet's trajectory, the smell of gunpowder. Yet, these fragments were locked in a disjointed mosaic. At times, the memories came back with such clarity that he felt detached, numb, as if the terror had been happening to someone else. The vividness of the details was accompanied by an emotional blankness that left him unable to weave them into a coherent narrative. The rigid posture that was supposed to bring safety instead reinforced a fractured recollection; the more he clung to the wall, the more his mind kept the memories isolated and unconnected, unable to form a continuous story of what had unfolded. Thomas's reliance on the wall and his heightened surveillance of people only deepened his sense that he had failed. The continuous monitoring of every passerby and the persistent rumination about exact revenge made him feel constantly on edge, convinced that the threat was real and that he could never truly be safe. His belief that he had not performed his duties adequately-his self-critical appraisal-was echoed back at him every time he sat with his back to the wall. The wall, once a source of perceived security, became a reminder of the very failure he feared. Each time he checked his surroundings, he felt the weight of his perceived inadequacy settle deeper into his chest, reinforcing the notion that he could not cope with even the slightest upset. The cycle-negative appraisal feeding maladaptive strategy, which in turn reinforces negative appraisal-tightened with each passing day. Today, Thomas finds himself unable to sleep. He wakes in the middle of the night, heart racing, hearing the imagined crack of a gun, and spends hours pacing the corridor before he can finally collapse on the floor, eyes wide open. The hypervigilance has seeped into his work; he no longer lets the courthouse doors open to a small group of protestors, fearing a repeat of the attack. He has begun avoiding long lines of people, even when they are not a threat, because the memory of that chaotic day lingers behind each face. Ruth has noticed his distance; she has asked him why he no longer talks about the day, and he has said he is trying to stay safe. He feels the world has turned into a maze of potential dangers that he cannot escape. The last week, a sudden siren outside the building startled him so violently that he almost ran from the office, only to be pulled back by Ruth's hand. It was this moment-his body racing, his mind spiraling, his heart beating against the walls of his own office-that finally pushed Thomas to seek help. He fears that if he does not learn to break the cycle, he will lose his job, his marriage, and perhaps his sense of self entirely. In therapy, he hopes to find a way to sit without the wall, to recall the event without the numbness, and to believe, if only a little, that he can cope with the ups and downs of a life still lived amid uncertainty.
